Where it began

Inzamam-ul-Haq was born in Multan on 3 March 1970, the youngest of five siblings. He began with his home-town side, Multan, in 1985, and later played for sides such as United Bank and National Bank.

The wider world met him at the 1992 World Cup. Imran Khan had chosen him for the trip to Australia and New Zealand, though few outside Pakistan knew the name. Then came the semi-final at Auckland. Chasing 262 with the game slipping away, the 22-year-old hit 60 from 37 balls and carried his side into the final, where a brisk 42 helped Pakistan lift the trophy.

The player

His Test debut came at Edgbaston in 1992, and swing bowling gave him a testing first summer. He learned quickly. At Karachi in 1994 he steered the tail home for a one-wicket win over Australia, and by 1995 he was ranked the best batsman in the world.

He played 120 Tests between 1992 and 2007, scoring 8,830 runs at 49.61 with 25 hundreds and 46 fifties. His best was 329 against New Zealand at Lahore in 2001–02, one of the biggest Test innings ever played by a Pakistani. He made 184 in his 100th Test, and in 2005 a hundred in each innings against England took him past Javed Miandad as Pakistan's leading maker of Test centuries. He captained his country in 30 Tests, winning 11.

What made him special

Inzamam picked up the length of the ball very early, then waited and played it late. He was quick on his feet for a big man, superb off his pads and one of the finest pullers of fast bowling anywhere. Against England he once passed fifty in nine innings in a row, a record against a single country. In the slips he was calm and soft-handed, and he held 81 Test catches.

The quick single was another matter. Running between the wickets was never his favourite part of the game, and a few of his run-outs became small comedies of their own. In one-day cricket only Marvan Atapattu was run out more often, and only by one.

Away from the middle

He was widely known as Inzi. In 2005 Pakistan awarded him the Sitara-e-Imtiaz. After his playing days he took charge of Afghanistan in 2015 and guided them to their first series win over a Test-playing nation, in Zimbabwe, and in 2016 he was appointed Pakistan's chief selector.

The family name lived on in the team. His nephew, Imam-ul-Haq, went on to play for Pakistan too.

And finally

He chose to bow out against South Africa in 2007, at the ground where his international career had started, needing 20 runs to pass Javed Miandad as Pakistan's highest Test run-scorer. He made 14 and then 3, and finished three runs short. Another 70 would have lifted his average to 50 as well. Cricket rarely ties a bow on a career, but it left him plenty to be proud of.
